title: Ashvamedhika
hook: the war is won, the funeral rites are done, and the new king falls down on the riverbank and can't get up

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the long sessions of Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma teaching from his bed of arrows, and then letting go. What stayed with you from all that advice? Today a new book opens. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

The water offerings for Bhishma have been poured into the Ganga. The great teacher is gone. Yudhishthira has listened to him at length, about kingship, about duty, about peace. He has the crown. He has the kingdom. And at the riverbank, in Ganguli's telling, he simply goes down, collapses on the bank, overwhelmed by grief. Bhima holds him. Krishna speaks to him. The old blind king Dhritarashtra, whose own sons died in this war, is the one who tells him to get up. A new book of the epic opens with a king on the ground. Its name is today's word.
screen: `THE OFFERINGS ARE POURED.` → `THE KING FALLS ON THE BANK.` → `THE BLIND KING SAYS: GET UP.`

segments.voice: Ashvamedhika is the book of the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice: a great royal rite in which a consecrated horse is let loose to wander, guarded by warriors, and the kingdoms it passes through either welcome it or fight. Yudhishthira doesn't come up with the idea. He wants to leave the throne and go to the forest. It's the sage Vyasa who tells him that grief is not a plan. Perform sacrifices, Vyasa says, give gifts, take up the work of a king; the horse sacrifice will cleanse what weighs on you. And Yudhishthira's answer is very practical. There's no money. The war has emptied the treasury. The kings who might have sent tribute are dead, and he will not squeeze grieving people for more. So Vyasa tells him an old story. Long ago, a king named Marutta held a sacrifice in the Himalayas so lavish that the gold left behind was too much to carry away. It's still there in the mountains, Vyasa says. Go and bring it. See what the epic is doing here. The victors don't get a parade. They get a man who can't stand up, a dead treasury, and a sage pointing at an old king's leftover gold. The way forward runs through someone else's generosity, long ago. Over the next days, this book will bring a forgotten teaching, an angry sage, a child who comes back to life, a son who fights his father, and a strange little animal with half a golden body. It begins with getting up.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHA: THE HORSE SACRIFICE` · `VYASA: GRIEF IS NOT A PLAN` · `"THE TREASURY IS EMPTY"` · then, large: `MARUTTA'S GOLD IN THE MOUNTAINS`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest open. Bring to mind a time you knew what you should do next and simply couldn't stand up to do it. You don't have to fix that time. Breathe in, and remember who helped you to your feet, or who you wish had. Breathe out, and let your shoulders drop. Then think of one person near you who may be on the riverbank right now. Just hold their name. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ashvamedhika. The book of the horse sacrifice, which begins with a grieving king and an empty treasury.
Your line: Ashvamedhika. Today, when someone near you is stuck on the riverbank, offer one practical thing, the way Vyasa did, not only comfort. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: The Ashvamedhika Parva is the book of the Mahabharata that follows Bhishma's teachings; Hindus hear it in recitations of the full epic, and the horse sacrifice is remembered as a great royal rite of the Vedic world.

match.prompt: the new book opens — tap the pairs.

myth: Yudhishthira proposes the horse sacrifice himself
he wants the forest; it's Vyasa who tells him to perform it.
the treasury is empty after the war
that's Yudhishthira's own objection to the sacrifice.
the gold for the rite comes from new taxes
Vyasa points to the gold King Marutta left in the mountains.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. Vyasa tells you to perform a great sacrifice, but the war has emptied your treasury and your people are grieving. what do you do?
options: raise taxes to pay for it.
tell Vyasa there's no money, and listen.
give up the throne for the forest.
fork.reveal: he says plainly there's no wealth and he won't press his people, and Vyasa answers with the story of Marutta's leftover gold.

original.note: ashvamedha: the horse sacrifice, the royal rite this book is named for.

trapdoor: what you thought: the book of the horse sacrifice is a victory celebration.
what it means: it opens with a king who can't get up and a treasury with nothing in it.
what a scholar hears: the rite is paid for with an old king's leftover gold, so the new reign starts on a gift from the past.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva, opening sections: Yudhishthira's grief at the Ganga, Dhritarashtra's and Krishna's counsel, Vyasa's advice, Marutta's wealth

notes: All paraphrase of Ganguli. Confirm the order of speakers at the opening (Yudhishthira falls on the Ganga's bank, Bhima holds him, Krishna and Dhritarashtra console him).
Confirm Yudhishthira's objection: the treasury exhausted by the war and his unwillingness to burden grieving subjects or demand tribute; wording here is a gloss.
Confirm Vyasa's framing that the sacrifice cleanses Yudhishthira of the burden of the war, and that Marutta's gold lies in the Himalayas.
The description of the ashvamedha (horse released to wander under guard) is general; a Keeper may wish to adjust it.
The teach previews later episodes of the book (Anugita, Uttanka, Parikshit, Babhruvahana, the mongoose) for the coming days.
Editor pass: 'for days' (unsourced length) changed to 'at length'; varied a 'Notice' opener used on nearby days.
Audit: read in full against Ganguli's sequence; no factual, framing or repetition problems found, no changes.
